title: Charles McGillivary's death at hands of Toronto police an accident, inquest rules
subtitle: Charles McGillivary died in 2011 after two Toronto police officers attempted to arrest him, mistaking him for another man with a similar physical description.
article: The jury at the coroner's inquest examining the death of Charles McGillivary, who died after being tackled by police in a case of mistaken identity, declared his death an accident on Thursday.

McGillivary, 45, died on Aug. 1, 2011, after two Toronto police officers attempted to arrest him, mistaking him for another man with a similar physical description who had allegedly breached his bail conditions.

Known as "Charlie" and "Lurch," McGillivary was developmentally challenged and hearing impaired. He fought back when police tried to handcuff him while he was walking with his mother, Ann, near Bloor St. and Christie St.
The 6-foot-4, 270-pound McGillivary, who suffered from a pre-existing heart condition, went into distress and was declared dead at Toronto Western Hospital.
The Special Investigations Unit cleared the two officers of any wrongdoing in 2012.

The coroner's inquest began earlier this month. The jury offered eight recommendations to help prevent similar deaths, including equipping police cars with automated external defibrillators (AED), and mouth shields and gloves to facilitate performing CPR and mouth-to-mouth resuscitation.
CPR was not performed on McGillivary until the paramedics arrived. Raymond Kang, one of the two officers, testified he wasn't sure it was needed.
The five jurors also want guidance for police to know if a person is not communicating due to a medical or cognitive disability.

Toronto police spokesman Mark Pugash, speaking on behalf of Deputy Chief Mike Federico, who appeared at the inquest, said police will look at the recommendations closely and "implement wherever it's reasonable to do so." He said there are currently no AEDs in police cars.

Jennifer Chambers, co-ordinator of the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health's empowerment council, which had standing at the inquest, said the council was generally pleased with the recommendations.

But she was disappointed the jury did not address McGillivary's mother's attempt to stop the officers the day her son was tackled. She approached them yelling, "That's my son Charlie!" but was ignored. Kang testified he was confused in the moment.
"She was treated quite harshly. She saw her son's death before her eyes. She's going to have to live with that," said Chambers.

The McGillivary family did not seek standing at the inquest. His death took a toll on the health of his mother and closest companion, Ann. Speaking to the Star earlier this month from a Nova Scotia hospital, she said she was not convinced the inquest would serve any real purpose.
"He's dead. Not going to bring him back."
